narrative:
The model predicted a 72.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had by far the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. At 23, it sits far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, and this large gap was the main reason the model saw a high risk of not passing the bar.

Your first-year grades in law school ranked second in importance. Placing in the 3rd decile—compared to an average of 6th decile among accepted students—also pulled the prediction toward failure, though less dramatically than the LSAT.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor. At 3.20 it is only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, and this small difference actually worked mildly in your favor, nudging the prediction slightly toward passing. However, it was not nearly enough to offset the much stronger negative signals from your LSAT and first-year performance.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as this had the greatest impact on the outcome. Stronger performance here, combined with continued solid grades, would likely change the prediction in future applications.
